question: What does the Bible say about free will?
intro: Christians read the Bible as calling people to choose, to repent and to obey, and also as telling of God at work in the human will, and they join the two in different ways when they ask how free a person is in turning to God. The phrase 'free will' comes from later Christian and philosophical writing; the Bible's own words are about choosing, willing, drawing, hardening and being unwilling. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them.

agreed.summary: Every reading below takes the text to address people as called to choose and answerable for what they choose, and takes any turning to God to rest on what God has first done. The readings differ in how they describe the human will itself, in how God's working and a person's choosing relate, and in whether the enabling to respond is given to everyone.

passages.quote: I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life, so that you and your descendants may live,
choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve
No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day.
We love because He first loved us.
For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose.

readings.label: Free choice, helped by grace: the will is wounded and not lost, and a person freely cooperates with God or refuses him
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to speak throughout to people who can answer, as when God sets a choice before Israel or Christ stands at the door and knocks. Catholic teaching holds that sin has wounded the human will without destroying its freedom, that grace moves and prepares the will, and that a person freely assents to this grace or resists it (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 5 and canons 4-5). Within Catholic teaching, schools differ on how God's moving of the will and the will's own assent fit together, and the Church has not decided between them. Eastern Orthodox readers hold that the freedom given with the image of God remains, and speak of a lifelong cooperation of the human will with God's grace (what is called synergy). The Confession of Dositheus (1672) holds that the fallen keep free will, can by nature choose and work moral good, and need grace for the good that leads to salvation, where the regenerate can will, or not will, to cooperate with grace. The Church of England's Article X says that after the fall a person cannot turn and prepare himself by his own strength, and that God's grace goes before the will and then works with it; many Anglicans hold part of this reading, and Anglican members differ among themselves in how they put it. Catholic and Orthodox writers also cite Sirach 15:14, a book outside the Protestant canon and outside the text quoted on this page.

passages.quote: If you do what is right, will you not be accepted? But if you refuse to do what is right, sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it.
passages.note: Read as God telling Cain that mastery is his to exercise (the Hebrew is hard, and translations differ).

passages.quote: If you are willing and obedient, you will eat the best of the land.
passages.note: A promise set on the people's willingness.

passages.quote: Cast away from yourselves all the transgressions you have committed, and fashion for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why should you die, O house of Israel?
passages.note: A command to the people to make a new heart for themselves.

passages.quote: how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!
passages.note: Christ's longing and the people's unwillingness, named side by side.

passages.quote: You stiff-necked people with uncircumcised hearts and ears! You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did.
passages.note: The Spirit can be resisted.

passages.quote: Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me.
passages.note: Christ knocks, and the opening is the hearer's.

passages.quote: And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.
passages.note: Read as saying that God gives the ability to stand.

passages.quote: Do not present the parts of your body to sin as instruments of wickedness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life; and present the parts of your body to Him as instruments of righteousness.
passages.note: Believers are told to present themselves, as an act of their own.

passages.quote: continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling
passages.note: The call to work out one's salvation, which comes just before 2:13 (“it is God who works in you”).

passages.quote: we are God's fellow workers
passages.note: Paul calls himself and Apollos God's fellow workers.

passages.quote: As God's fellow workers, then, we urge you not to receive God's grace in vain
passages.note: Paul, as God's fellow worker, urges them not to receive God's grace in vain.

passages.quote: See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God
passages.note: A warning that no one fall short of the grace of God.

passages.quote: Return to Me, declares the LORD of Hosts, and I will return to you
passages.note: A call to return to the LORD, with the promise that he will return to the people.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take the verses that say no one can come unless the Father draws or grants it (John 6:44, 6:65) and the promise of a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26-27) to speak of the grace that moves and strengthens the will and does not set it aside. They take Romans 8:7 and John 8:34 to describe a will wounded by sin and inclined toward it, which grace heals, and they read Romans 8:7's 'nor can it do so' as the wound of the will and not its loss. They take Proverbs 16:9, Proverbs 21:1 and Genesis 50:20 to speak of God's providence working through and alongside human choices, and they read Exodus 9:12 together with Exodus 8:15, where Pharaoh first hardens his own heart.

readings.label: A will that chooses as it wills, and wills as its nature leads (what is called the bondage of the will): God's working changes the will so that it turns to him
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to say that every person chooses what he most wants, and answers for it, and that fallen human nature leaves the will unwilling to turn to God until God works in it. Lutheran and Reformed readers hold this under names of their own (the bondage of the will, shared by both; and, among many Reformed readers and some Lutheran ones, compatibilism, the view that God's ordering of events and a person's own choosing are both true), with a shared concern that God alone be the source of a person's turning. Many Lutherans leave how God's working and a person's choosing fit together as a mystery the text does not explain. Lutheran teaching grants the will some liberty in civil matters and none in spiritual ones (Augsburg Confession XVIII), holds that the Spirit works faith through the Word and sacraments and is resisted by those who persistently reject the Word (Solid Declaration II), and the Missouri Synod's Brief Statement says that non-conversion is due to the person alone and that why some are converted and others not belongs to God's judgments. Lutheran and Reformed readers differ from each other on whether the Spirit's work can finally be resisted. Baptists of the 1689 London Confession (chapter 9) state this reading, and many Anglicans read the Church of England's Article X in this sense; other members of those traditions hold the others. How far sin reaches in a person, and whom God chooses, are the subject of other pages.

passages.quote: Truly, truly, I tell you, everyone who sins is a slave to sin.
passages.note: Read as saying that sin binds the one who practices it.

passages.quote: because the mind of the flesh is hostile to God: It does not submit to God's law, nor can it do so.
passages.note: A mind that does not submit and cannot.

passages.quote: This is why I told you that no one can come to Me unless the Father has granted it to him.
passages.note: Coming to Christ as something the Father grants.

passages.quote: And I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes and to carefully observe My ordinances.
passages.note: Spoken to Israel as a promise of restoration; these holders read it of the Spirit's work in believers.

passages.quote: in the hope that God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth.
passages.note: Repentance spoken of as God's grant.

passages.quote: A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps.
passages.note: The person plans and the LORD determines, in one sentence.

passages.quote: The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul's message.
passages.note: God opens the heart, and the response follows.

passages.quote: As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this-to preserve the lives of many people.
passages.note: One act, two intentions: the brothers' and God's.

passages.quote: you were dead in your trespasses and sins
passages.note: The condition of a person before God acts: dead in trespasses and sins.

passages.quote: made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses
passages.note: God made those who were dead in trespasses alive with Christ.

passages.quote: There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God.
passages.note: No one understands and no one seeks God.

passages.quote: if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed
passages.note: If the Son sets a person free, that person is free indeed; it follows 8:34, which is on this card.

passages.quote: The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them
passages.note: The natural man does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, and cannot understand them.

passages.quote: apart from Me you can do nothing
passages.note: Jesus says that apart from him his disciples can do nothing.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take the commands to choose and to repent (Deuteronomy 30:19, Joshua 24:15, Ezekiel 18:31, Acts 17:30) to state what people owe God, and the promises of a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26-27) to supply what is commanded. They take Matthew 23:37 and Acts 7:51 to describe real refusals, willed by those who made them and answered for. They take Revelation 3:20 as an invitation which the Spirit makes effective in those he brings to open the door. They read 1 Timothy 2:4 and Titus 2:11 in more than one way (as offered to every kind of person, or as God's revealed wish alongside his purpose), and Reformed and Lutheran readers do not read them alike. They read Exodus 9:12 with Exodus 4:21, where the LORD says he will harden Pharaoh's heart, and with Exodus 8:15, where Pharaoh hardens his own, as one event described from two sides.

readings.label: Grace that frees every person to respond (what is called prevenient grace): the bound will is freed by God, and the answer is the person's own
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to say two things at once: that apart from God no one can come, and that God has given to everyone the grace that makes a response possible, so that the response is real and can be refused. Wesleyan and Methodist readers call this prevenient grace, grace that comes before any decision. Article VIII of the United Methodist Church's Articles of Religion says that no one can turn and prepare himself without the grace of God 'preventing us', and Wesley's sermons speak of this grace as given to every person. Anabaptist readers, who mostly speak in other terms, put weight on the call to a free, adult decision to follow Christ; the 1995 Mennonite confession says that human beings have free will though choice is limited, that the Holy Spirit moves people to accept the gift of salvation, and that God brings people into right relationship without coercion. The Assemblies of God uses the term prevenient grace in its 2017 position paper on the assurance of salvation, and Pentecostal and Charismatic members mostly stand here. Among Baptists, the Free Will Baptist Treatise says that the power to believe is the gift of God and that believing is an act of the creature; the Baptist Faith and Message (2000) of the Southern Baptist Convention does not choose between this reading and the second, and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (chapter 9) states the second. Many other Baptist and free-church members hold this reading, including those who speak of the freedom of the will. Anglican members hold this reading in part, in the words of Article X, which speaks of grace that goes before ('preventing') the will and then works with it, and they differ among themselves on whether that grace is given to everyone. Members of these traditions differ among themselves in how far they spell it out.

passages.quote: The true Light, who gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.
passages.note: Light given to every person.

passages.quote: And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself.
passages.note: Read as the drawing of John 6:44, given to all.

passages.quote: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone.
passages.note: Saving grace appearing to everyone.

passages.quote: who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
passages.note: God's wish for everyone.

passages.quote: Although God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times, He now commands all people everywhere to repent.
passages.note: A command to all, taken to imply the ability to answer it.

passages.quote: Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.
passages.note: The call to whoever calls, in the words the early church took from Joel.

passages.quote: And let the one who is thirsty come, and the one who desires the water of life drink freely.
passages.note: An open invitation to whoever desires.

passages.quote: If anyone desires to do His will, he will know whether My teaching is from God or whether I speak on My own.
passages.note: A will turned toward God's will and the knowing that follows.

passages.quote: God's kindness leads you to repentance
passages.note: God's kindness leads a person to repentance.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take Romans 8:7, John 8:34, John 6:44 and John 6:65 to be true of every person apart from God's prior grace, and take John 1:9, John 12:32 and Titus 2:11 to name that grace as given to all, so that the bound will is freed to respond. They take Proverbs 16:9, Proverbs 21:1 and Genesis 50:20 to speak of God's rule over events and his working with willing hearts, without making the choice for the person. They take Acts 11:18 and 2 Timothy 2:25 to say that repentance is God's gift, which a person receives or refuses, and they read Exodus 9:12 together with Exodus 8:15, where Pharaoh first hardens his own heart.

terms.note: The Lutheran and Reformed phrase for the teaching that, after the fall, the human will is unwilling to turn to God until God works in it.

A philosophers' term, used by many Reformed readers and some Lutheran ones, for the view that God's ordering of events and a person's own free choosing are both true of the same act. The Westminster Confession, the standard of the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church, states the substance in its own words (3.1, 9.1): God's ordering of events takes away neither the will's liberty nor the contingency of second causes.
The term used in Lutheran and Reformed teaching for the view that God alone works to bring a person to faith.
The Catholic term for the human power to choose, which Catholic teaching holds is wounded by sin and not lost.
The Eastern Orthodox term for the human will cooperating with God's grace.

The Wesleyan term for grace that comes before any human decision and makes a response possible; the Assemblies of God uses it in its 2017 position paper on the assurance of salvation; Article X of the Church of England speaks of grace 'preventing' us in the older sense of going before; Catholic teaching speaks in its own terms of a grace that comes before, and the Council of Trent uses the phrase 'prevenient grace of God' itself (Session 6, chapter 5).

A philosophers' term, used by many holders of the third reading and by some of the first, for the power to choose otherwise given the same circumstances; Lutheran and Reformed readers describe the freedom of the will in other terms.

The name of a fifth-century teaching that grace is not needed to begin or to complete obedience, which church councils rejected; the word is often used as a charge between traditions, and holders of each reading above deny that it describes them. Article VII of the Methodist Articles of Religion names the Pelagians in rejecting the teaching that original sin consists in the following of Adam, 'as the Pelagians do vainly talk'.

further_reading.title: Council of Trent, Session 6, Decree on Justification, chapter 5 and canons 4-5
further_reading.says: It teaches that grace comes first and that a person can receive the Holy Spirit's inspiration or reject it, that no one can by his own free will move himself to justice without God's grace, and it condemns the view that free will was lost and extinguished by Adam's sin or that the will does not cooperate.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1731-1738 (Man's Freedom: Freedom and Responsibility)
further_reading.says: It teaches that freedom is the power, rooted in reason and will, to choose and act deliberately, and that this makes a person responsible for what he does voluntarily.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1739-1742 (Man's Freedom: Human Freedom in the Economy of Salvation)
further_reading.says: Paragraph 1742 teaches that grace does not compete with human freedom, and that through grace the Holy Spirit forms people in spiritual freedom so that they can cooperate freely.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1996-2005 (Grace and Justification: Grace), especially 2001-2002
further_reading.says: It teaches that God's grace prepares a person to receive it and sustains the person's cooperation (2001), and that God's free initiative calls for a free human response (2002).

further_reading.title: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672), Decrees 3 and 14
further_reading.says: Decree 14 says that the fallen keep free will, can by nature choose and work moral good, and need grace for spiritual works toward salvation, and that a person has it in his power to will, or not to will, to cooperate with grace; Decree 3 speaks of a preventing grace imparted to all and of use to the willing.

further_reading.title: The Longer Catechism of Philaret of Moscow, questions 123 and 162
further_reading.says: Question 162 says God gave the first people a will naturally inclined to love God and yet free, and question 123 says God gives all people preparatory grace and sufficient means to reach happiness.

further_reading.title: Augsburg Confession, Article XVIII (Of Free Will)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the human will has some liberty to choose civil righteousness and to work things subject to reason, and no power without the Holy Spirit to work the righteousness of God.

further_reading.title: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article II (Free Will)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the unconverted will cannot understand, believe or prepare itself for grace, that the Holy Spirit alone brings conversion through the Word and the sacraments, and that those who persistently reject the Spirit's work through the Word resist him (paragraphs 58-60, 83).

further_reading.title: Luther's Small Catechism, The Creed, the Third Article
further_reading.says: It teaches that a person cannot by his own reason or strength believe in Jesus Christ or come to him, and that the Holy Spirit has called the believer by the Gospel.

further_reading.title: Martin Luther, On the Bondage of the Will (De servo arbitrio, 1525)
further_reading.says: Luther's reply to Erasmus's treatise on free will, and the work from which the phrase 'bondage of the will' comes.

further_reading.title: A Brief Statement of the Doctrinal Position of the Missouri Synod (1932), Article 7 (Of Conversion)
further_reading.says: It teaches that conversion is the work of God's grace and almighty power alone, that a person's non-conversion is due to himself alone, and that why some are converted and others not belongs to God's unsearchable judgments.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 9 (Of Free Will), with chapter 3.1 and chapter 10.1
further_reading.says: Chapter 9 says God gave the will a natural liberty that is neither forced nor determined by any absolute necessity of nature, and that by the fall man lost all ability of will to any spiritual good; chapter 3.1 says no violence is offered to the will of creatures and the liberty of second causes is not taken away.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Shorter Catechism, question 31
further_reading.says: It teaches that effectual calling is the Holy Spirit's work, in which he opens our minds to know Christ and renews our wills so that we are persuaded and able to receive him.

further_reading.title: Canons of Dort, Third and Fourth Main Points of Doctrine (Human Corruption and Conversion to God), articles 3, 10-12 and 16
further_reading.says: It teaches that no one can turn to God without the Spirit's regenerating work, that conversion is to be credited to God, and that regeneration neither abolishes the will nor coerces a reluctant will by force (article 16).

further_reading.title: Heidelberg Catechism, questions 8 and 9
further_reading.says: Question 8 says that we are so corrupt that we are wholly unable to do any good unless we are born again by the Spirit of God, and question 9 says God created human beings with the ability to keep the law and that they lost it by their own disobedience.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 2, chapter 2 (Man now deprived of freedom of will, and miserably enslaved)
further_reading.says: Calvin holds that sin has taken possession of the human will so that a person cannot choose good unaided, and that the will acts without outward compulsion, so that people are called free because they act willingly.

further_reading.title: Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion, Article X (Of Free-Will)
further_reading.says: It says that after the fall a person cannot turn and prepare himself to faith and calling on God by his own natural strength and good works, and that good works pleasing to God need God's grace going before and then working with us once we have a good will.

further_reading.title: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church, Articles VII and VIII
further_reading.says: Article VIII says that after the fall a person cannot turn and prepare himself to faith by his own strength and has no power to do good works acceptable to God without the grace of God by Christ preventing us, and Article VII names the Pelagians in rejecting the view that original sin consists in following Adam.

further_reading.title: Global Methodist Church, Doctrinal Standards: the Articles of Religion and the Confession of Faith
further_reading.says: It confirms the Articles of Religion as doctrinal standards of the Global Methodist Church.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Standard Sermons, Sermon 43 (The Scripture Way of Salvation), part 1
further_reading.says: Wesley defines preventing grace as all that is wrought in the soul by what is often called natural conscience, and speaks of the convictions the Spirit works in every child of man, most of which people stifle.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Sermon 85 (On Working Out Our Own Salvation)
further_reading.says: Wesley teaches that a person is by nature spiritually dead and cannot move toward God until God acts, that no one is in a state of pure nature since everyone receives preventing grace, and that because God works in people to will and to act they are able to work out their salvation.

further_reading.title: James Arminius, A Declaration of the Sentiments of Arminius (1608), section 3 (The Free Will of Man), the Arminian source of the Wesleyan reading
further_reading.says: Arminius holds that in his fallen state a person is not capable of himself to think, will or do what is really good, and must be regenerated and renewed by God in intellect, affections and will; once renewed he can think, will and do good, with God's continuing grace.

further_reading.title: Second London (Baptist) Confession of 1689, chapter 9 (Of Free Will)
further_reading.says: Paragraph 3 says that by the fall a person has lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation, and paragraph 4 says that in conversion God frees the sinner from bondage to sin and by grace alone enables him to will and do what is spiritually good.

further_reading.title: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article III (Man) and Article V (God's Purpose of Grace)
further_reading.says: Article III says man was created with freedom of choice and that only the grace of God can bring him into fellowship with God, and Article V says election is consistent with the free agency of man; the text names neither prevenient grace nor the bondage of the will.

further_reading.body: National Association of Free Will Baptists
further_reading.title: Treatise on the Faith and Practice of the Free Will Baptists (2026 edition)
further_reading.says: It says that the call of the gospel extends to all through the Word and the Spirit's strivings, and that the power to believe is the gift of God while believing is an act of the creature.

further_reading.title: Assemblies of God position paper, The Assurance of Salvation (2017), section I
further_reading.says: It names prevenient grace as the grace God provides before salvation, drawing all people toward salvation and enabling them either to accept or to reject his offer.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 7 (Sin), commentary 4
further_reading.says: The commentary says that although human beings have free will, choice is limited, and that by God's grace they can choose the bond of covenant relationship with God.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 8 (Salvation), commentary
further_reading.says: It says that the Holy Spirit moves us to accept the gift of salvation and that God brings us into right relationship without coercion.

_why: QUOTES: every quote was read against http://localhost:8012/api/verse and ticked. Deut 30:19 (from 'I have set before you'; the verse begins 'I call heaven and earth as witnesses'), Josh 24:15 (clause), John 6:44 (opening curly quote dropped), 1 John 4:19, Phil 2:13, Gen 4:7 (closing curly quote dropped), Isa 1:19, Ezek 18:31, Matt 23:37 (clause), Acts 7:51, Rev 3:20, 1 Cor 10:13 (whole verse after 'No temptation has seized you...'), Rom 6:13, John 8:34 (clause from 'Truly'), Rom 8:7, John 6:65 (clause, curly quotes dropped), Ezek 36:27, 2 Tim 2:25 (clause), Prov 16:9, Prov 21:1, Gen 50:20 (the server's hyphen kept), John 1:9, John 12:32 (closing curly quote dropped), Titus 2:11, 1 Tim 2:4 (a clause continuing 2:3), Acts 17:30, Heb 3:15 (clause), Rev 22:17 (clause), John 7:17. Verses cited by reference only, in 'answers', were also read on the server: Ezek 36:26, Exod 8:15, Exod 9:12, Acts 11:18. ORDER: by when each reading was set out. First the reading of the early church and its heirs (the Greek fathers' language of free choice and the Catholic statements that followed); second the line from the late Augustine to the Reformers and the Reformed confessions; third the reading that sets out grace as freeing every person, whose main form dates from the early 1600s and the 1700s, though the Anabaptist emphasis on free decision is from the 1520s. The order is by history and does not rank. WHY THREE: the usual split is 'free will' against 'predestination', which has no place for a third position held by large traditions (Wesleyan, Pentecostal, much of the free church): its holders say, with the second reading, that the will is bound without grace, and, with the first, that the answer to grace is the person's own. SCOPE: whom God chooses for salvation is left to the card 'election', and how deep sin reaches in a person to 'total-depravity'. Some verses sit near all three (John 6:44, John 6:65, Rom 8:7); I used them only where the question is the will and the card cannot leave them out. Exod 9:12 is not quoted, only referred to in 'answers', where the first and third readings take it with 8:15 and the second takes the hardening and Pharaoh's own as one event; the second reading's 'answers' does not say so because it is not a reading of that verse the card attributes to it, a reviewer may add it. PASSAGES: 5 in the common ground, 8 in each reading, equal. HELD_BY: approximate, and the summaries say where members differ. Anglican is in 1 and 2 (the Anglican articles speak in both ways); Baptist / free church in 2 and 3 (Calvinistic and General Baptists differ, said in the summaries); Pentecostal / Charismatic only in 3 (there are Reformed Charismatics, covered by 'mostly'); Anabaptist only in 3. No person, scholar or leader is named anywhere in the card. WORDS: I scanned the summaries, answers, labels and notes for 'but', 'however', 'actually', 'clearly', 'only', 'merely'; none appears outside the verses' own words ('but' occurs inside quotes such as Gen 4:7 and Prov 16:9, which is the verse). 'Mostly' in reading 3 is hedged for the reasons above; a reviewer may check it. LEFT OUT: (a) Jer 13:23 (the Ethiopian's skin and the leopard's spots), the classic text for an inability to change, was removed on purpose: a reader outside the US Christian mainstream, and an African American reader especially, would meet a comparison between a people's skin and entrenched evil; Rom 8:7 and John 8:34 carry the same point. (b) Rom 7:14-25 (7:18 'I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out'), which each reading takes differently (Paul before Christ, Paul the believer, or any person struggling); it belongs on the total-depravity or human-nature card. (c) Eph 2:1, Rom 3:10-12, Rom 9 and Acts 13:48, left to total-depravity and election. (d) Deut 30:11-14 ('this commandment is not too difficult for you'), which a rabbi may want in the first reading, as Jewish readers take Deut 30 as the plainest statement that choice is within reach; I held to 30:19 for the count and a reviewer may swap. (e) The fall (Gen 3), left to the human-nature card; Gen 4:7 stays because it speaks directly of mastering sin. (f) Phil 2:12 (in faith-and-works), 1 Cor 9:24-27, Rom 2:4. (g) Divine foreknowledge (Rom 8:29, Acts 2:23) and secular determinism, a separate question. (h) Jewish and Islamic accounts of choice: the card is about how Christians disagree. READERS: a Catholic reader may want the wording of the Council of Trent, which is not quoted because only the Bible's text is; the idea is in the summary. An Eastern Orthodox reader may object that 'wounded' is a Western word, so the summary says the freedom 'remains' for them. A Lutheran may object that the second reading puts Lutheran and Reformed teaching in one place; the summary notes they differ on resisting the Spirit, and the Lutheran distinction between freedom in earthly matters and bondage in spiritual ones is not drawn. A rabbi will note that the OT passages (Deut 30:19, Gen 4:7, Isa 1:19, Ezek 18:31) are quoted in their own settings, words to Israel and to Cain, and that Jewish readers take them as plainly about choice. A young African American believer: 'slave to sin' (John 8:34) is the verse's own word and the note says 'binds'; the card uses neither 'slave' nor 'freedom' in a political or American sense, and the site's theme 'freedom' (being set free) is related. A secular scholar will see that the card says what the readings are and not which came to be the larger.
